fixes.explanation: You've got it, baker. The fat goes up on the altar, and the breast goes to Aaron and his sons. The person presenting the offering brings it with his own hands and waves the breast before the LORD (Leviticus 7:30). Then verse 34 calls the breast a permanent portion for the priests, so the waving ends with the priests getting it.

Nice try, but lighting it fresh would mean the fire went out first, and verse 12 says it "…must not be extinguished." What the priest does each morning is add wood to the fire that's already burning. Honestly, I'd love to be the priest on that shift. Walk up, bring the wood, and the fire says, "Oh, you're here? I've been up all night."

Right, baker. The priest who offers the sin offering is the one who eats it, in a holy place, in the courtyard of the Tent of Meeting (Leviticus 6:26). The text calls it most holy. So no eating on the run and no snacking while you walk. When I'm holding a tray of cookies, I never get that kind of focus.

Right, friend. A clay pot used to boil the sin offering must be broken. If it's boiled in a bronze pot instead, that pot must be scoured and rinsed with water (Leviticus 6:28). Two kinds of pot, two instructions. Bronze gets a scrub and clay gets broken, so I'm glad I only deal with cookie sheets.

Good guess, friend, because elders feel like the right people to pass a message down the line. But verse 23 has the LORD tell Moses, "Speak to the Israelites and say…" Moses speaks to the Israelites themselves, so the fat command lands on everybody with no middleman. If this had been a game of telephone, I'd have wanted a shorter line too.

Good guess, friend, because Passover is a big one in Israel's story. But verse 38 names a different command for that day: the LORD "…commanded the Israelites to present their offerings to the LORD in the Wilderness of Sinai." That fits, since this whole passage is about offerings. The Passover feast just isn't what the verse is talking about.
